claim: Participants plan at least two future reaches simultaneously with an ongoing reach.
source: We show that participants plan at least two future reaches simultaneously with an ongoing reach.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from target jump experiments (Figure 3) and IRI measurements (Figure 2).

claim: The planning processes of two future reaches are not independent of one another.
source: Further, the planning processes of the two future reaches are not independent of one another.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing slower corrections in H3 vs H2 conditions (Figure 4).

claim: Correcting for a visual perturbation of the ongoing reach target is slower when more future reaches are planned.
source: First, correcting for a visual perturbation of the ongoing reach target is slower when more future reaches are planned.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from the +1 target jump experiment comparing H2 and H3 conditions (Figure 4).

claim: The curvature of the current reach is modified based on the next reach only when their planning processes temporally overlap.
source: Second, the curvature of the current reach is modified based on the next reach only when their planning processes temporally overlap.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by curvature analysis data showing co-articulation effects only in H3+ conditions (Figure 6).

claim: Interactions between future planning processes may enable smooth production of sequential actions by linking individual segments of a long sequence at the level of motor planning.
source: These interactions between future planning processes may enable smooth production of sequential actions by linking individual segments of a long sequence at the level of motor planning.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Many everyday actions like speaking or preparing a cup of tea are composed of long and often rapid sequences of movements.
source: Many everyday actions like speaking or preparing a cup of tea are composed of a long and often rapid sequences of movements (Lashley, 1951).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lashley, 1951.

claim: For successful performance of sequential tasks, the next movement needs to be proactively planned before the previous movement is concluded.
source: For successful performance of such tasks, the next movement needs to be proactively planned before the previous movement is concluded.
evidence: This is based on logical inference from the nature of sequential movements and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Prior investigations in saccadic eye movements show that sequence production is faster and more efficient when participants have access to information that allows them to plan future movements.
source: Indeed, prior investigations in saccadic eye movements (McPeek et al., 2000; McPeek and Keller, 2002), reading (Rayner, 1998), walking (Patla and Vickers, 2003), typing (Snyder and Logan, 2014), finger movements (Ariani et al., 2021; Ariani et al., 2020; Shahbazi et al., 2024), path tracking (Bashford et al., 2022), target harvesting (Diamond et al., 2017), and reaching (Howard et al., 2015; Säfström et al., 2014; Zimnik and Churchland, 2021) consistently show that sequence production is faster and more efficient when participants have access to information that allows them to plan the future movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research across different motor domains.

claim: The nervous system has the ability to plan future movements while executing the current movement (online planning).
source: This improvement demonstrates the nervous system's ability to plan future movements while executing the current movement – i.e., to do online planning (Ariani et al., 2021; Ariani et al., 2020; Ariani and Diedrichsen, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on online planning.

claim: Planning and execution-related processes of a single movement occur in overlapping brain areas and often are carried out by the same neurons.
source: Planning and execution-related processes of a single movement occur in overlapping brain areas and often even carried out by the same neurons (Crammond and Kalaska, 2000; Elsayed et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2014), so an important question is how the nervous system avoids interference between the planning of a future movement and the control of the current one when producing rapid sequential movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: In monkey primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), preparation of the next movement occurs in an orthogonal neural subspace to that which controls the ongoing movement.
source: In a short sequence of two reaches, Zimnik and Churchland, 2021 proposed that in monkey primary motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), preparation of the next movement occurs in an orthogonal neural subspace to that which controls the ongoing movement, thereby allowing these two processes to run in parallel without interference.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zimnik and Churchland, 2021.

claim: It remains unknown to what degree multiple future reaches are planned and whether these planning processes interact with each other and with the ongoing action.
source: It remains unknown to what degree multiple future reaches are planned, and whether these planning processes interact with each other and with the ongoing action.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Participants performed sequences of 14 reaches in a planar robotic exoskeleton.
source: Participants were instructed to perform sequences of 14 reaches in a planar robotic exoskeleton.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The targets were generated from a hexagonal grid of potential targets with radii of 1 cm spaced 4 cm apart over a 21×24 cm2 total workspace.
source: The targets were generated from a hexagonal grid of potential targets with radii of 1 cm spaced 4 cm apart over a 21×24 cm2 total workspace (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Participants captured each target by staying within it for 75, 200, or 400 ms (dwell time).
source: They captured each target by staying within it for 75, 200, or 400 ms (dwell time, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Longer dwell times required a full stop in each target, while shorter dwell times allowed participants to link subsequent reaches into a co-articulated unit.
source: Longer dwell times required a full stop in each target, while shorter dwell times allowed participants to link subsequent reaches into a co-articulated unit (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation about the effect of dwell time on movement kinematics, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: IRI was significantly reduced from Horizon 1 to Horizon 2 for all dwell times.
source: IRI was significantly reduced from Horizon 1 to Horizon 2 for all dwell times.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The average reduction of IRI from H1 to H2 was 206 ms for 75 ms dwell time (t(10) = 22.76, p=3.02e-10).
source: The average reduction of IRI was 206 ms (t(10) = 22.76, p=3.02e-10), 232 ms (t(10) = 27.41, p=4.83e-11), and 246 ms (t(10) = 24.84, p=1.27e-10) for the 75, 200, and 400 ms dwell times, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The average reduction of IRI from H1 to H2 was 232 ms for 200 ms dwell time (t(10) = 27.41, p=4.83e-11).
source: The average reduction of IRI was 206 ms (t(10) = 22.76, p=3.02e-10), 232 ms (t(10) = 27.41, p=4.83e-11), and 246 ms (t(10) = 24.84, p=1.27e-10) for the 75, 200, and 400 ms dwell times, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The average reduction of IRI from H1 to H2 was 246 ms for 400 ms dwell time (t(10) = 24.84, p=1.27e-10).
source: The average reduction of IRI was 206 ms (t(10) = 22.76, p=3.02e-10), 232 ms (t(10) = 27.41, p=4.83e-11), and 246 ms (t(10) = 24.84, p=1.27e-10) for the 75, 200, and 400 ms dwell times, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A further small 16 ms improvement in IRI was observed from H2 to H3 in the 75 ms dwell time condition (t(10) = 3.137, p=5.30e-3).
source: We also observed a further small 16 ms improvement from H2 to H3 in the 75 ms dwell time condition (t(10) = 3.137, p=5.30e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The IRI results suggest that, at least for a dwell time of 75 ms, participants plan two targets ahead of the current reach.
source: These results suggest that, at least for a dwell time of 75 ms, participants plan two targets ahead of the current reach.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the IRI data showing improvement from H2 to H3.

claim: The +2 target was occasionally displaced when the current (+0) target was captured in the target jump experiment.
source: That is, we occasionally displaced the target two reaches in the future (i.e. the +2 target) when the current (i.e. +0) target was captured.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation in the target jump experiment.

claim: If information about the +2 target was not being used, both the movement toward the unperturbed +1 target and to the jumped +2 target should not differ from unperturbed conditions.
source: If information about the +2 target was not being used, we would expect to see no interruption in the sequence: both the movement toward the unperturbed +1 target, as well as to the jumped +2 target should not differ from unperturbed conditions (Figure 3B, solid line).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that the +2 target is not being planned.

claim: The reach time to the +1 target was not reliably different between the jump and no-jump conditions (t(9) = 0.63, p=0.54).
source: The reach time to the +1 target was not reliably different between the jump and no-jump conditions (t(9) = 0.63, p=0.54; Figure 3C, Execution +1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Dwell time inside the +1 target was not reliably different between jump and no-jump conditions (t(9) = 1.98, p=0.08).
source: This was also true for dwell time inside the +1 target (t(9) = 1.98, p=0.08; Figure 3C, Dwell +1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Movement time from the +1 to the +2 target was significantly longer in the jump condition (t(9)=5.90, p=2.00e-4).
source: However, movement time from the +1 to the +2 target was significantly longer in the jump condition (t(9)=5.90, p=2.00e-4; Figure 3C, Execution +2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Participants reached toward the pre-jump +2 target, and then corrected their reach toward the new position of +2 target.
source: However, this explanation is not consistent with our kinematic analysis which revealed participants reached toward the pre-jump +2 target, and then corrected their reach toward the new position of +2 target (Figure 3B, dotted line).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinematic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The minimum distance between reach trajectory and center of pre-jump +2 target was significantly lower in the jump condition (t(9)=5.78, p=3.00e-4).
source: The minimum distance was significantly lower in the jump condition (t(9)=5.78, p=3.00e-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of kinematic data.

claim: The reach to the +2 target was at least partially planned before the target jump, simultaneous with the reach to the +0 target and planning of the reach to the +1 target.
source: Together with the speedup of the overall movement (Figure 2), these results show that the reach to the +2 target was at least partially planned before the target jump, simultaneous with the reach to the +0 target and planning of the reach to the +1 target (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the target jump experiment results and IRI data.

claim: The position of the +1 target was jumped when the +0 target was captured to test whether two future movement plans interact.
source: We tested whether two future movement plans interact by jumping the position of the +1 target when the +0 target was captured.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation to test interaction between planning processes.

claim: If the +1 and +2 targets are planned independently, the movement correction to a displacement of the +1 target should be the same in the H2 and H3 conditions.
source: If the +1 and +2 targets are planned independently, the movement correction to a displacement of the +1 target should be the same in the H2 and H3 conditions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis of independent planning.

claim: If the movements interact, the correction should be slower in the H3 condition because some of the resources would be assigned to planning the +2 target.
source: Alternatively, if the movements interact – if they are planned together or share limited resources – the correction should be slower in the H3 condition because some of the resources would be assigned to planning the +2 target.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis of interacting planning processes.

claim: The corrections for a +1 target jump were longer and slower in the H3 condition than in the H2 condition.
source: Consistent with an interaction between future plans, we found that the corrections for a +1 target jump were longer and slower in the H3 condition than in the H2 condition (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In both H2 and H3 conditions, participants failed to correct the movement before arriving at the pre-jump position of the +1 target.
source: In both conditions, participants failed to correct the movement before arriving at the pre-jump position of the +1 target (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the H3 condition, both the movement time (t(9) = 4.85, p=1.80e-3) and the trajectory length (t(9) = 6.19, p=3.00e-4) of the corrective movement were longer than that of the H2 condition.
source: In the H3 condition, both the movement time (t(9) = 4.85, p=1.80e-3) and the trajectory length (t(9) = 6.19, p=3.00e-4) of the corrective movement were longer than that of the H2 condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The corrective reaches were closer to the center of the +2 target in H3 condition (t(9) = 4.28, p=4.00e-3).
source: The corrective reaches were closer to the center of the +2 target in H3 condition (t(9) = 4.28, p=4.00e-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: It took more time to update the +1 movement plan when participants could simultaneously plan both the +1 and +2 target as compared to when they could only plan the +1 target.
source: In summary, it took more time to update the +1 movement plan when participants could simultaneously plan both the +1 and +2 target as compared to when they could only plan the +1 target.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the +1 target jump experiment.

claim: Planning a reach to the +2 target occupied some part of a shared computational resource such that less of the resource was available for updating the reach to the +1 target.
source: This effect indicates that planning a reach to the +2 target occupied some part of a shared computational resource such that less of the resource was available for updating the reach to the +1 target.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings suggesting shared resources.

claim: The experimental results indicate a clear interaction between the planning processes for future movements.
source: These results indicate a clear interaction between the planning processes for future movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the +1 target jump experiment results.

claim: An extreme version of interaction between future reaches is that they are planned as a single unit, as a 'motor chunk'.
source: An extreme version of such an interaction is that the two future reaches are planned as a single unit, as a 'motor chunk' (Figure 5B; Ramkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about chunked planning, supported by a citation to Ramkumar et al., 2016.

claim: The experimental data are not consistent with the idea that future reaches are planned as a motor chunk.
source: Our data, however, are not consistent with the idea that future reaches are planned as a motor chunk.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results that contradict the chunking hypothesis.

claim: An important indicator of chunking is that, after a chunk is executed, there is a short delay until the next chunk is planned.
source: First, an important indicator of chunking is that, after a chunk is executed, there is a short delay until the next chunk is planned.
evidence: This is a statement about expected characteristics of chunked planning based on prior knowledge.

claim: Except for H1 condition, the speed profiles of other horizon conditions showed no evidence of pauses between reaches.
source: However, except for H1 condition, where the participants had to pause and wait for the next target to appear, the speed profiles of other horizon conditions showed no evidence of such pauses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of speed profiles shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chunked planning predicts that a disturbance in any segment of the chunk would affect the whole chunked segment.
source: Second, chunked planning predicts that a disturbance in any segment of the chunk would affect the whole chunked segment.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the chunking hypothesis.

claim: When the +2 target was jumped, participants performed the reach to the +1 target in a manner identical to the no-jump condition (t(9) = 0.60, p=0.56).
source: When we jumped the +2 target, the participants performed the reach to the +1 target in a manner identical to the no-jump condition (t(9) = 0.60, p=0.56).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When the +1 target was jumped, participants still went through the pre-jump +1 target but their movement was significantly shortened by deviating toward the new position of the +1 target (t(9) = 14.36, p=1.64e-7).
source: Additionally, when we jumped the +1 target they still went through the pre-jump +1 target but their movement was significantly shortened by deviating toward the new position of the +1 target (t(9) = 14.36, p=1.64e-7) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Participants were able to correct the second segment of their movement without causing any disturbance in the first segment.
source: In summary, participants were able to correct the second segment of their movement without causing any disturbance in the first segment.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the target jump experiments.

claim: The ability to correct the second segment without disturbing the first provides clear evidence against chunked planning of the future reaches.
source: This observation provides clear evidence against chucked planning of the future reaches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Interactions among planning processes could allow the motor system to optimize the set of movements leading to systematic co-articulation of movement segments.
source: The experiments above indicate that reach planning to the +1 and +2 targets interact with each other. Such interactions could allow the motor system to optimize the set of movements leading to systematic co-articulation of movement segments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional consequence of planning interactions.

claim: When the visual information of the future target is available, each movement in the sequence could be planned in a way that accounts for the movement that comes after it.
source: In other words, when the visual information of the future target is available, each movement in the sequence could be planned in a way that accounts for the movement that comes after it.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how co-articulation might arise from planning interactions.

claim: Systematic co-articulation of movements was observed in the H3 condition.
source: Indeed, we observed systematic co-articulation of movements in the H3 condition (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When the +2 target demanded an upcoming rightward turn, the +1 reach curved left, and vice versa.
source: When the +2 target demanded an upcoming rightward turn, the +1 reach curved left, and vice versa (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Although the deviation led to a longer overall trajectory, it reduced the required turning angle at the +1 target.
source: Although this deviation led to a longer overall trajectory, it reduced the required turning angle at the +1 target.
evidence: This is an observation about the biomechanical consequence of the curvature effect.

claim: In the H1 and H2 conditions, the slope of curvature effect was not reliably different from zero, indicating no systematic co-articulation.
source: In the H1 and H2 conditions, the slope was not reliably different from zero, indicating no systematic co-articulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: The absence of curvature effect in H2 suggests that co-articulation of segments cannot happen if planning of the next segment happens during the execution of the previous one.
source: Notably, we did not observe the curvature effect in the H2 condition in which the +2 target was on the screen only during the execution of the +1 reach. This suggests that co-articulation of segments cannot happen if planning of the next segment happens during the execution of the previous one.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of curvature effect in H2 condition.

claim: In the H3 condition, the slope was reliably smaller than zero for all the dwell time conditions, indicating systematic co-articulation once parallel planning was feasible.
source: In the H3 condition, the slope was reliably smaller than zero for all the dwell time conditions, indicating systematic co-articulation once parallel planning was feasible.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: In the case of the 75 ms dwell time, the co-articulation kept growing from H3 to H4 (t(10) = 5.54, p=2.60e-03).
source: In the case of the 75 ms dwell time, the co-articulation kept growing from H3 to H4 (t(10) = 5.54, p=2.60e-03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: No reliable increase in co-articulation was observed for Horizon>3 for the 200 ms dwell time (t(10) = 0.19, p>0.98).
source: We observed no reliable increase in co-articulation for Horizon>3 for the 200 ms (t(10) = 0.19, p>0.98) or 400 ms dwell times (t(10) = 0.38, p>0.99).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: No reliable increase in co-articulation was observed for Horizon>3 for the 400 ms dwell time (t(10) = 0.38, p>0.99).
source: We observed no reliable increase in co-articulation for Horizon>3 for the 200 ms (t(10) = 0.19, p>0.98) or 400 ms dwell times (t(10) = 0.38, p>0.99).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: Less co-articulation was observed for longer dwell times.
source: Overall, we observed less co-articulation for longer dwell times.
evidence: This is a summary observation from the curvature analysis across dwell times.

claim: With longer dwell times, the overall rise and saturation of the curvature effect was smaller (F(2,20) = 16.71, p=6.00e-04).
source: However, with longer dwell times, the overall rise and saturation of the curvature effect was smaller (F(2,20) = 16.71, p=6.00e-04), suggesting less interaction between planning processes when the movements are biomechanically separated.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of curvature data.

claim: The biomechanically advantageous co-articulation between segments of the sequence occur when the segments are planned together.
source: Together, these results show that the biomechanically advantageous co-articulation between segments of the sequence occur when the segments are planned together.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the curvature analysis results.

claim: In ~95% of all reaches in all trials, participants made only one saccade per reach.
source: We found that in ~95% of all reaches in all trials, participants made only one saccade per reach, indicating they primarily focused on the immediate next target with information about subsequent targets likely being processed through parafoveal vision.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: Participants primarily focused on the immediate next target with information about subsequent targets likely being processed through parafoveal vision.
source: We found that in ~95% of all reaches in all trials, participants made only one saccade per reach, indicating they primarily focused on the immediate next target with information about subsequent targets likely being processed through parafoveal vision.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eye-tracking data showing one saccade per reach.

claim: The saccade to the next target occurred after the current target disappeared, and right before the hand exited the disappeared target.
source: The saccade to the next target occurred after the current target disappeared, and right before the hand exited the disappeared target.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: The relative timing between the saccade and the hand exiting the target was consistent across different horizons (F(2,36) = 1.92, p=0.16).
source: The relative timing between the saccade and the hand exiting the target was consistent across different horizons (F(2,36) = 1.92, p=0.16).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: Saccade angle is shifted toward the position of the future target in the H2 and H3 conditions.
source: As shown in one representative participant (Figure 7C), we found that saccade angle is shifted toward the position of the future target in the H2 and H3 conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At the group level, the saccade angle was significantly different for different horizons (F(8,128) = 12.60, p=3.12e-13).
source: At the group level, the saccade angle was significantly different for different horizons (F(8,128) = 12.60, p=3.12e-13).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: In Horizon 1, the average saccade angle for different targets was identical since the future target was not shown.
source: In Horizon 1, as expected, the average saccade angle for different targets was identical since the future target was not shown.
evidence: This is an observation from the eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: For both Horizon 2 and Horizon 3, the angle of the saccade was systematically shifted toward the position of the upcoming target.
source: For both Horizon 2 and Horizon 3, the angle of the saccade was systematically shifted toward the position of the upcoming target.
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: Information about future targets is received parafoveally, and the fixation location is systematically shifted to facilitate this process.
source: Together, these results suggest that information about future targets is received parafoveally, and the fixation location is systematically shifted to facilitate this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the eye-tracking data analysis.

claim: In a previous finger sequence study using a similar horizon manipulation, participants executed sequences faster when they had information about multiple future finger presses.
source: In a previous finger sequence study, using a similar horizon manipulation to the one used here, we found that participants executed sequences faster when they had information about multiple future finger presses (Ariani et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research by Ariani et al., 2021.

claim: In the previous finger sequence study, the benefit of future information increased up to horizon of three future finger presses (H3) and then plateaued.
source: This benefit increased up to horizon of three future finger presses (H3) and then plateaued.
evidence: This is a description of findings from prior research cited in the discussion.

claim: The more pronounced effect of horizon on movement speed in finger presses may be attributed to the nature of the effectors, as future finger flexions can commence in advance.
source: Another possible reason for the more pronounced effect of horizon on movement speed in finger presses may be attributed to the nature of the effectors. Specifically, in reaching movements, the arm cannot initiate the next reach before completing the previous one. In contrast, with finger movements, future finger flexions can commence in advance, potentially resulting in faster execution of the sequence (Popp et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between finger and reaching tasks, supported by a citation to Popp et al., 2022.

claim: The difference between finger and reaching tasks may arise because the transformation of the visual cue to motor plans is faster for the direct spatial mapping used in reaching than for the more abstract number-to-finger mapping used in finger sequences.
source: It is also possible that this difference arises because the transformation of the visual cue to motor plans is faster for the direct spatial mapping used here than for the more abstract number-to-finger mapping used in our previous study (Diedrichsen et al., 2001; Goodman and Kelso, 1980).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior research on cue-to-action mapping.

claim: The availability of the second reach target can be more significant when faster execution of the task demands faster transformation of visual cue to muscle commands, or when the cue-to-action mapping is more demanding.
source: Overall, these observations suggest that the availability of the second reach target can be more significant when faster execution of the task demands faster transformation of visual cue to muscle commands, or when the cue-to-action mapping is more demanding.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from comparing the current results with prior finger sequence studies.

claim: In the work by Ames et al., 2019, target displacement during execution led to an initial commitment to the pre-jump position of the target followed by a smooth corrective reach toward the new target position.
source: This behavior is similar to that shown in the work by Ames et al., 2019, where target displacement during execution led to an initial commitment to the pre-jump position of the target followed by a smooth corrective reach toward the new target position.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ames et al., 2019.

claim: Ames et al., 2019 showed that resource distribution in M1 and PMd is accomplished by re-planning the corrective reach in a subspace orthogonal to the one controlling the ongoing movement.
source: Neurally, the authors showed that resource distribution in M1 and PMd is accomplished by re-planning the corrective reach in a subspace orthogonal to the one controlling the ongoing movement (Ames et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ames et al., 2019.

claim: One possibility for the interaction between planning processes is that the neural resources dedicated to re-planning have to be split between preparation of future targets, slowing the re-planning of the next movement.
source: One possibility is that the neural resources dedicated to re-planning have to be split between preparation of future targets, slowing the re-planning of the next movement (Kornysheva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed interaction, supported by a citation to Kornysheva et al., 2019.

claim: Another possibility for the interaction is that the two future movements may be prepared as a chunk, and changing the entire chunk may take longer time than changing a single movement.
source: Alternatively, the two future movements may be prepared as a chunk (Ramkumar et al., 2016), and changing the entire chunk may take longer time than changing a single movement.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Ramkumar et al., 2016.

claim: By probing the planned state with target perturbations, the study clearly demonstrates an obligatory interaction between multiple future movement plans.
source: Either way, by probing the planned state with target perturbations we clearly demonstrate an obligatory interaction between multiple future movement plans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the target perturbation experiments.

claim: The observed curvature interaction can be either due to fully chunked planning of two elements, or alternatively, due to separate, yet interactive, planning of the two reaches.
source: The observed curvature interaction can again be either due to fully chunked planning of two elements, or alternatively, due to separate, yet interactive, planning of the two reaches.
evidence: This presents two possible interpretations of the curvature findings.

claim: Fully chunked planning seems less likely because the interaction was observed even when movement segments were fully separated by a long dwell time.
source: The former possibility seems less likely since the interaction was observed even when movement segments were fully separated by a long dwell time (Figure 6D, Dwell 400).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the curvature data showing effects even with long dwell times.

claim: Previous neurophysiological investigations showed that individual neurons can be involved in both the planning and execution phases of a movement.
source: Previous neurophysiological investigations showed that individual neurons can be involved in both the planning and execution of phases of a movement (Churchland and Shenoy, 2007; Crammond and Kalaska, 2000; Elsayed et al., 2016; Kaufman et al., 2014; Pruszynski et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior neurophysiological research.

claim: When two movements are concatenated, the planning of the second movement can proceed in parallel with the control of the first movement.
source: Nonetheless, when two movements are concatenated, the planning of the second movement can be proceeded in parallel with the control of the first movement.
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings on parallel planning and execution.

claim: The lack of interference between planning and execution can be explained by the fact that planning and execution proceed in orthogonal neural subspaces.
source: This lack of interference can be explained by the fact that planning and execution proceed in orthogonal neural subspaces (Zimnik and Churchland, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zimnik and Churchland, 2021.

claim: One hypothesis is that the two future movements are planned in orthogonal neural subspaces without any interactions during the planning phase, and co-articulation arises from interaction between execution dynamics and planning dynamics.
source: One hypothesis is that the two future movements are also planned in orthogonal neural subspaces without any interactions during the planning phase. Under this hypothesis, the co-articulation we report would arise from an interaction between the execution dynamics associated with the current movement and the planning dynamics of the second planned movement.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the neural mechanism underlying co-articulation.

claim: An alternative hypothesis is that the preparation processes of the next two movements directly interact with each other, and possibly are even encoded partly together.
source: An alternative hypothesis is that the preparation processes of the next two movements directly interact with each other, and possibly are even encoded in partly together (Fusi et al., 2016; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to Fusi et al., 2016 and Rigotti et al., 2013.

claim: The results are suggestive of the hypothesis that preparation processes directly interact since no co-articulation was observed when the next target was only available during execution of the current reach.
source: Our results are suggestive of the latter scheme since we observed no co-articulation when the next target was only available during execution of the current reach (Figure 6D, H2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the curvature data to support one hypothesis over another.

claim: Careful electrophysiology experiments are necessary to investigate the exact mechanism by which planning processes interact.
source: Nevertheless, careful electrophysiology experiments are necessary to investigate the exact mechanism by which planning processes interact.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The current paradigm provides a useful framework for investigating neural mechanisms of planning interactions.
source: The current paradigm provides a useful framework to do so.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the experimental paradigm for future research.

claim: Previous studies found participants keep their visual attention on the current sequence item and can perceive the location of spatial targets even when foveal vision is occluded.
source: This observation aligns with previous studies (Clavagnier et al., 2007; González-Alvarez et al., 2007; Sivak and MacKenzie, 1990) that found participants keep their visual attention on the current sequence item and can perceive the location of spatial targets even when foveal vision is occluded.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on visual attention during reaching.

claim: Changes in gaze location were observed even in Horizon 2, despite no changes in the curvature of hand movements in this horizon.
source: Notably, changes in gaze location were observed even in Horizon 2, despite no changes in the curvature of hand movements in this horizon (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation comparing eye movement and hand movement data.

claim: Information about the next target may first be available in the circuitry that controls eye movements and later in the cortical areas that control voluntary upper limb movements.
source: This suggests that information about the next target may first be available in the circuitry that controls eye movements and later in the cortical areas that control voluntary upper limb movements.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the dissociation between eye and hand movement changes.

claim: Further control studies are required to investigate the hypothesis about differential timing of information availability in eye and hand control circuits.
source: Further control studies are required to investigate this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Eleven participants (4 female) with an average age of 23.3 years (4.4 SD years) completed five experimental visits for the study.
source: Eleven participants (4 female) with an average age of 23.3 years (4.4 SD years) completed five experimental visits for this study (~10 hr data collection per participant); this data was used for IRI (Figure 2) and curvature analysis (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample for the main experiments.

claim: Ten of the eleven participants returned for two experimental visits where they were tested on target jump experiments.
source: Ten of these participants returned for two experimental visits where they were tested on target jump experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample for the jump experiments.

claim: The eleven participants were all right-handed with average handedness of 78 (24 SD), measured by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: They were all right-handed with average handedness of 78 (24 SD), measured by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: For eye position analysis, a different group of 20 right-handed participants (2 female) with average age of 21.2 years (2.0 SD years) was recruited.
source: For eye position analysis, we recruited a different group of 20 right-handed participants (2 female) with average age of 21.2 years (2.0 SD years), one participant was excluded from the analysis due to low quality of data (see Eye-tracker analysis below).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample for the eye-tracking experiments.

claim: One participant from the eye-tracking group was excluded from the analysis due to low quality of data.
source: For eye position analysis, we recruited a different group of 20 right-handed participants (2 female) with average age of 21.2 years (2.0 SD years), one participant was excluded from the analysis due to low quality of data (see Eye-tracker analysis below).
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria.

claim: All participants reported no prior history of musculoskeletal, neurological, or psychiatric disorders.
source: All participants reported no prior history of musculoskeletal, neurological, or psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Health Sciences Research Ethics Board at the University of Western Ontario (Project ID 115088).
source: All the procedures were approved by the Health Sciences Research Ethics Board at the University of Western Ontario (Project ID 115088).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: Participants performed all experimental trials in an exoskeleton robot (Kinarm, Kingston, ON, Canada).
source: Participants performed all experimental trials in an exoskeleton robot (Kinarm, Kingston, ON, Canada).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Arm kinematics were recorded at 1000 Hz.
source: Arm kinematics were recorded at 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection method.

claim: Participants' eye movement was recorded using an SR Research Eyelink 1000 at 1000 Hz.
source: Participants' eye movement was recorded using an SR Research Eyelink 1000 at 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the eye-tracking apparatus and sampling rate.

claim: The sequences always started from a fixed home target in the center of the working space.
source: The sequences always started from a fixed home target in the center of the working space.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Sequences were generated according to two rules: the next target should be a neighbor of the previous target, and there were no loops smaller than five reaches.
source: We generated sequences according to two rules. First, the next target in the sequence should be a neighbor of the previous target. This ensured that all the reaches were 4 cm apart. Second that there were no loops smaller than five reaches. This ensured that, when multiple future targets were presented, they did not overlap.
evidence: This is a description of the sequence generation algorithm.

claim: The entire experiment had seven sessions.
source: The entire experiment had seven sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The first five sessions were designed to get time and curvature analysis in all dwell and horizon conditions.
source: The first five sessions were designed to get a time and curvature analysis in all dwell and horizon conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The last two sessions added the jump experiment.
source: The last two session added the jump experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each of the first five sessions consisted of three blocks of 120 trials for each dwell time, with horizon randomized across trials totaling 360 trials per session.
source: Each session consisted of three blocks of 120 trials for each dwell time, and the horizon was randomized across trials totaling 360 trials per session.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each session of data collection was 1 hr and 15 min on average.
source: Each session of data collection was 1 hr and 15 min on average.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: IRI is defined as the time the hand entered one target until it entered the next one.
source: For the analysis of movement time, we computed IRI, defined as the time the hand entered a one target until it entered the next one.
evidence: This is a definition of a measurement used in the analysis.

claim: For curvature analysis, only reaches with five potential future choices were considered to ensure participants could not predict the overall position of the upcoming target.
source: However, near the boundaries of the workspace, the number of potential next targets decreases so the participants could potentially predict the overall position of the upcoming target and plan for it ahead of time (Glaser et al., 2018). To ensure that this possibility did not affect our results, we only considered reaches with five potential future choices.
evidence: This is a description of data selection criteria to control for potential confounds, supported by a citation to Glaser et al., 2018.

claim: The +1 jump experiment consisted of 400 trials, 200 target jumps in H2 and H3, interleaved with 200 no-jump trials randomized across horizons.
source: The +1 jump experiment consisted of 400 trials, 200 target jumps in H2 and H3, interleaved with 200 no-jump trials with randomized across horizons.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for the +1 jump experiment.

claim: The +2 jump experiment was performed only in Horizon 3 (H3) condition with a total of 300 trials.
source: The +2 jump experiment was performed only in Horizon 3 (H3) condition. There was a total of 300 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for the +2 jump experiment.

claim: In the +2 jump experiment, two-thirds of trials were no jump; in the remaining one-third, the +2 target jumped to a new position when the +0 target was captured.
source: Two-third of them were no jump; in the remaining one-third, exactly at the movement that the current target (+0 target) was captured, the second future target (+2 target) jumped to a new position, and the position of the next target (+1 target) remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for the +2 jump experiment.

claim: For eye-tracker pre-processing, trials were removed if the eye position was not recorded for a consecutive 600 ms.
source: For pre-processing of eye-tracker data, we first removed trials if the eye position was not recorded for a consecutive 600 ms.
evidence: This is a description of data preprocessing criteria.

claim: In 95% of the trials only one saccade happened in each reach.
source: In 95% of the trial only one saccade happened in each reach.
evidence: This is a description of the eye-tracking data analysis results.

claim: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA was employed for analysis of IRI and curvature effect with factors of dwell time (three levels), horizon (five levels), and their interaction.
source: For analysis of IRI and curvature effect, we used two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Factors were dwell time (three levels), horizon (five levels: H1 to H5), and (dwell time × horizon) interaction.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis method.

claim: P-values for multiple comparisons were adjusted using Holm method.
source: For comparison between different levels of each significant factor, we adjusted p-values for multiple comparisons using Holm method.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical correction method.
